title: Dona Veneris. Clipeus
titleEn: Venus's Gift and the Pictures on the Shield — Aeneid VIII.608–731
part: Venus's Gift and the Pictures on the Shield (VIII.608–731)
about: Aeneas has ridden with his picked men to the grove near Caere, close to where the Etruscans are camped, and the book ends with the gift his mother promised him. Venus finds him alone in a secluded valley, shows herself openly, embraces him, and lays the armour Vulcan has forged under an oak: now he need not hesitate to challenge the Laurentines and Turnus. Aeneas cannot look enough at the helmet that spouts flame, the sword, the blood-red breastplate, the greaves and the spear, and above all the shield, on which the god of fire, who knew what the prophets had foretold, has worked the story of Rome to come. The scenes follow one another in order: the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus in the cave of Mars; the Sabine women seized at the games, the war that followed and the treaty sworn at Jupiter's altar; the traitor Mettus torn apart by chariots; the Etruscan king Porsenna besieging Rome to bring back the banished Tarquin, while Cocles breaks down the bridge and Cloelia swims the Tiber; Manlius holding the Capitol against the Gauls when a silver goose gives the alarm; the dancing priests of Mars and the holy shields fallen from heaven; and the underworld, with Catiline punished and Cato giving laws to the righteous. In the centre, ringed by a golden sea where silver dolphins play, is the battle of Actium in 31 BC: Augustus with the Senate, the people and the gods of Rome, his admiral Agrippa beside him, and against them Antony with the wealth of the East and his Egyptian queen, Cleopatra, the beast-headed gods of Egypt fighting the gods of Rome, until Apollo bends his bow and the whole East turns and runs, and the queen flees into the arms of the grieving Nile. Last comes Augustus's triple triumph at Rome, the thanksgiving in every temple, and the conquered nations of the world filing past him in procession. Aeneas understands none of it; he delights in the pictures, and lifts onto his shoulder the glory and the destiny of his descendants.

advisory.lede: Among the scenes on the shield, this part shows the Sabine women carried off by the first Romans from the games to be their wives (635–636), and the traitor Mettus torn apart between two chariots (642–645).
advisory.more: Both are pictures worked in metal, each told in a few lines. The Sabine women are named in a single phrase, 'raptas sine more', 'seized against all custom', and the poem moves at once to the war their kinsmen made and the treaty that ended it; nothing of what happened to the women is described. Mettus's punishment takes about three lines: the chariots pulling him apart, King Tullus dragging the liar's entrails through a wood, the brambles dripping with blood. The text is presented unaltered, and the translations and notes render what the Latin says at the force it says it.

sentences.t:
At Venus aetherios inter dea candida nimbos
dona ferens aderat;
sentences.l:
But Venus, among the ethereal, the goddess shining, clouds,
bringing gifts, was at hand;
sentences.i: But Venus, the shining goddess, came among the clouds of heaven bearing her gifts;
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, the last of Book 8. 'At', 'but', turning from the Etruscan camp to the goddess. 'aetherios inter… nimbos', 'among the clouds of the upper air', the preposition set between adjective and noun, and 'dea candida', 'the bright goddess', set inside the frame. 'dona ferens', 'bringing gifts': the arms she asked Vulcan to make (8.370 ff.) and he forged (8.424 ff.), and promised Aeneas by the sign in the sky (8.534–536). 'aderat', 'was at hand', 'arrived'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
natumque in valle reducta
ut procul egelido secretum flumine vidit,
talibus adfata est dictis seque obtulit ultro:
sentences.l:
and her son, in a valley withdrawn,
when far off by the chill, apart, stream she saw,
with such she addressed him words and herself offered unasked:
sentences.i: and when she saw her son far off, alone in a secluded valley by the cool stream, she spoke to him in these words and showed herself to him of her own accord:
sentences.n: 'natumque… ut… vidit', 'and when she saw her son', 'ut' with the perfect indicative meaning 'when'; 'natum' is pulled ahead of 'ut' for emphasis. 'valle reducta', 'in a valley drawn back', secluded. 'egelido… flumine', 'by the chill stream', framing 'secretum', 'apart', set aside from his men; 'egelidus' can mean either 'with the chill taken off' or 'very cold', and here, by a shady grove, it is cool (L&S gives both). 'talibus… dictis', 'with such words', framing. 'adfata est', 'addressed', from the deponent 'adfor' (Greenough's spelling of 'affata', the prefix unassimilated). 'seque obtulit ultro', 'and offered herself unasked': in Book 1 she met him disguised as a huntress, and he knew her only as she turned to go (1.402–406); now she comes openly. Elisions 'natumqu(e) in', 'adfat(a) est', 'sequ(e) obtulit'.

sentences.t:
“En perfecta mei promissa coniugis arte
munera, ne mox aut Laurentis, nate, superbos
aut acrem dubites in proelia poscere Turnum.”
sentences.l:
“Look, finished by my husband's skill, the promised
gifts, so that soon neither the Laurentines, son, the proud,
nor fierce Turnus you may hesitate to battle to challenge.”
sentences.i: “Here are the gifts I promised, finished by my husband's skill, so that you need not hesitate, my son, to challenge the proud Laurentines or fierce Turnus to battle before long.”
sentences.n: Venus's speech, the whole of it in three lines, opening and closing in this unit. 'En', 'see!', presenting something. 'perfecta… munera', 'gifts completed', framing across the line-end; 'promissa' agrees with 'munera', 'the promised gifts'. 'mei… coniugis arte', 'by the craft of my husband', Vulcan, the smith of the gods. 'ne… dubites', 'so that you may not hesitate', a negative purpose clause with the present subjunctive. 'Laurentis… superbos', 'the proud Laurentines', '-is' accusative plural, the Latins of King Latinus's city Laurentum; 'aut… aut', 'either… or', here after a negative, 'neither… nor'. 'nate', vocative, 'son'. 'in proelia poscere', 'to call out to battle'. 'coniugis', with consonantal i, 'con-ju-gis'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Dixit et amplexus nati Cytherea petivit,
arma sub adversa posuit radiantia quercu.
sentences.l:
She spoke, and the embraces of her son Cytherea sought;
the arms under the facing she set, gleaming, oak.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the goddess of Cythera sought her son's embrace, and laid the gleaming armour beneath an oak that faced him.
sentences.n: 'Dixit', 'she spoke', closing the speech. 'amplexus… petivit', 'sought the embraces', 'amplexus' accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun. 'nati', 'of her son'. 'Cytherea', Venus, from the island of Cythera; the 'y' is short, Cy-the-re-a. In Book 1 Aeneas complained that his mother never let him join his hand to hers (1.408–409); here she embraces him. 'sub adversa… quercu', 'under the oak opposite', enclosing 'posuit radiantia'. 'radiantia', 'gleaming', with 'arma'. The second clause follows without a connective. Behind the scene is Iliad 19, where Thetis brings Achilles the armour Hephaestus made for him (from memory). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ille, deae donis et tanto laetus honore,
expleri nequit atque oculos per singula volvit
miraturque interque manus et bracchia versat
terribilem cristis galeam flammasque vomentem
fatiferumque ensem,
sentences.l:
He, with the goddess's gifts and so great an honour delighted,
cannot be filled, and his eyes over each thing rolls,
and marvels, and between his hands and arms turns
the terrible with crests helmet, and flames spewing,
and the fate-bearing sword,
sentences.i: Delighted with the goddess's gifts and with so great an honour, he cannot have his fill, but runs his eyes over every piece, marvelling, and turns over in his hands and arms the helmet with its fearsome crest, spouting flames, and the death-dealing sword,
sentences.n: A comma-ended unit: the sentence runs on to 625, a list of the arms one by one. 'Ille', Aeneas. 'deae donis… laetus', 'glad at the goddess's gifts', ablatives of cause with 'laetus'. 'expleri nequit', 'cannot be filled', present passive infinitive: he cannot look enough, as Dido could not at 1.713. 'per singula', 'over each single thing'. 'oculos… volvit', 'rolls his eyes'. 'miraturque interque', the double '-que'; 'inter… manus et bracchia', 'between hands and arms', i.e. in his hands and arms. 'terribilem cristis galeam', 'a helmet terrible with crests', 'cristis' ablative of cause. 'flammas… vomentem', 'spewing flames', a sign of the hero's power in battle. 'fatiferum', 'fate-bearing', deadly, a compound adjective. Elisions 'atqu(e) oculos', 'miraturqu(e) interque', 'fatiferumqu(e) ensem'.

sentences.i: the breastplate, stiff with bronze, blood-red and huge, like a dark cloud when it kindles in the sun's rays and glows far and wide;
sentences.n: 'loricam ex aere rigentem', 'a breastplate stiff from bronze', 'ex' of the material. 'sanguineam ingentem', 'blood-red, huge', two adjectives side by side without a connective; the colour is the glow of the metal, explained by the simile. 'qualis cum', 'such as when', a short simile. 'caerula nubes', 'a dark-blue cloud', 'caeruleus' covering the dark colours of sea and sky. 'solis… radiis', 'with the rays of the sun', ablative of means, framing 'inardescit', 'takes fire'. 'refulget', 'shines back', reflects. Elisions 'loric(am) ex', 'sanguine(am) ingentem'.

sentences.t:
tum levis ocreas electro auroque recocto
hastamque et clipei non enarrabile textum.
sentences.l:
then the smooth greaves of electrum and gold re-smelted,
and the spear, and of the shield the not-to-be-told fabric.
sentences.i: then the smooth greaves of electrum and refined gold, the spear, and the fabric of the shield, past all telling.
sentences.n: 'tum', 'then', in the list. 'levis ocreas', 'smooth greaves', 'lēvis' with a long e, 'smooth', '-is' accusative plural; greaves are the shin-guards. 'electro', 'electrum', pale gold alloyed with silver, and 'auro… recocto', 'gold smelted again', refined; ablatives of material. 'clipei non enarrabile textum', 'the not-to-be-recounted fabric of the shield': 'textum', 'woven thing', of the shield's layers and pictures worked together; 'enarrabilis', 'that can be told in full'. 'clipei' is three syllables, cli-pe-i. The description of the shield follows to the end of the book. It answers Homer's shield of Achilles (Iliad 18, from memory), which shows the whole world, cities at peace and at war, ploughing, harvest and dance; Virgil's shows the history of Rome to come. Elisions 'electr(o) auroque', 'hastamqu(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Illic res Italas Romanorumque triumphos
haud vatum ignarus venturique inscius aevi
fecerat ignipotens, illic genus omne futurae
stirpis ab Ascanio. pugnataque in ordine bella.
sentences.l:
There the Italian story and the Romans' triumphs,
not of the prophets ignorant nor unknowing of the age to come,
had made the Fire-lord; there all the race of the future
stock from Ascanius, and the fought-out in order wars.
sentences.i: There the lord of fire, who knew the prophets' words and the age to come, had wrought the history of Italy and the triumphs of the Romans; there was all the line to spring from Ascanius, and the wars they fought, one after another.
sentences.n: The print has 'ab Ascanio. pugnataque', a full stop before a lowercase word, a misprint for a comma, corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. The '-que' adds the wars to the list governed by 'fecerat'. 'Illic', 'there', on the shield. 'res Italas', 'Italian affairs', the history of Italy. 'triumphos', victory processions through Rome. 'haud vatum ignarus venturique inscius aevi', 'not ignorant of the seers nor unknowing of the age to come': 'haud' negates both adjectives. 'ignipotens', 'mighty in fire', Vulcan's title; Greenough prints it lowercase here and with a capital at 710. 'genus omne futurae stirpis ab Ascanio', 'the whole race of the stock to come from Ascanius', the Julian line, which claimed him as ancestor under his other name, Iulus. Elisions 'vat(um) ignarus', 'venturiqu(e) inscius', 'pugnataqu(e) in'.

sentences.t:
Fecerat et viridi fetam Mavortis in antro
procubuisse lupam, geminos huic ubera circum
ludere pendentis pueros et lambere matrem
impavidos, illam tereti cervice reflexa
mulcere alternos et corpora fingere lingua.
sentences.l:
He had made also, in the green, of Mavors, cave, the new-mothered
she-wolf lying down; the twin, around her udders,
to play hanging, boys, and to lick their mother
unafraid; her, with smooth neck bent back,
to caress them in turn and their bodies to shape with her tongue.
sentences.i: He had made, too, the she-wolf that had just given birth, stretched out in the green cave of Mars, with the twin boys hanging at her teats, playing and nuzzling their mother without fear, while she bent back her smooth neck and caressed each in turn, shaping their bodies with her tongue.
sentences.n: The first picture. Romulus and Remus, twin sons of Mars and the Vestal virgin Rhea Silvia (Ilia), were exposed by the usurping king of Alba Longa and suckled by a she-wolf in a cave under the Palatine, the Lupercal (8.343). 'Fecerat et', 'he had made also': from here each scene is something Vulcan 'had made', often with accusative and infinitive ('lupam procubuisse'), which makes the picture move. 'Mavortis… in antro', 'in the cave of Mavors', the old name of Mars, the boys' father. 'fetam', 'having newly given birth'. 'huic ubera circum', 'around her udders', 'circum' after its noun, 'huic' (one syllable) dative. 'pendentis', '-is' accusative plural with 'pueros'. 'tereti cervice reflexa', ablative absolute, 'her smooth neck bent back'. 'fingere lingua', 'to shape with her tongue', as animals were believed to lick their young into shape. Elision 'mulcer(e) alternos'.

sentences.t:
Nec procul hinc Romam et raptas sine more Sabinas
consessu caveae magnis circensibus actis
addiderat subitoque novum consurgere bellum
Romulidis Tatioque seni Curibusque severis.
sentences.l:
Not far from here Rome, and the seized, without custom, Sabine women
from the seated crowd of the stands, the great Circus games being held,
he had added, and suddenly a new rising war
for the sons of Romulus and for old Tatius and for stern Cures.
sentences.i: Not far from this he had added Rome, and the Sabine women carried off, against every custom, from the crowded stands when the great games of the Circus were held, and a new war suddenly springing up between the sons of Romulus and old Tatius with his stern people of Cures.
sentences.n: Romulus's new city had no wives; the Romans invited the Sabines with their families to games and at a signal seized the girls (Livy 1, from memory). 'raptas sine more', 'seized without custom', outside every rite of marriage. 'consessu caveae', 'from the seated assembly of the stands', the 'cavea' being the banked seating; ablative of separation. 'magnis circensibus actis', ablative absolute, 'the great Circus games being held', named after the games of Virgil's own day. 'addiderat', 'had added', with the infinitive 'consurgere', 'a new war rising', as with 'fecerat'. 'Romulidis', 'for the sons of Romulus', the Romans, a patronymic, dative. 'Tatio… seni', Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, who made war to win the women back. 'Curibus… severis', 'for stern Cures', the Sabine town (plural in form) standing for its people; the Sabines were proverbial for austerity. Elision 'Rom(am) et'.

sentences.t:
Post idem inter se posito certamine reges
armati Iovis ante aram paterasque tenentes
stabant et caesa iungebant foedera porca.
sentences.l:
Afterwards the same, between them their contest laid aside, kings,
armed, of Jupiter before the altar and bowls holding,
were standing, and, a sow slain, were joining treaties.
sentences.i: Afterwards the same kings, their quarrel laid to rest, stood armed before the altar of Jupiter holding sacrificial bowls, and sealed a treaty with the slaughter of a sow.
sentences.n: 'idem… reges', 'the same kings', Romulus and Tatius, 'idem' nominative plural. Peace came when the Sabine women, now wives and mothers, ran between the two armies; the peoples were joined, and the two kings ruled together (Livy 1, from memory). 'inter se posito certamine', ablative absolute, 'the struggle between them laid down'. 'Iovis ante aram', 'before the altar of Jupiter', the genitive set ahead of the preposition; 'Iovis' with consonantal i. 'pateras', shallow bowls for pouring offerings of wine. 'caesa… porca', ablative absolute, 'a sow having been slain', the old victim when a treaty was struck. 'iungebant foedera', 'were joining treaties'. The imperfects 'stabant… iungebant' show the scene in progress. Elisions 'id(em) inter', 'ant(e) aram'.

sentences.t:
Haud procul inde citae Mettum in diversa quadrigae
distulerant, at tu dictis, Albane, maneres,
raptabatque viri mendacis viscera Tullus
per silvam, et sparsi rorabant sanguine vepres.
sentences.l:
Not far from there swift, Mettus in different directions, four-horse chariots
had torn apart (but you to your words, Alban, should have held!),
and was dragging of the lying man the entrails Tullus
through the wood, and, spattered, were dripping with blood the brambles.
sentences.i: Not far from there, four-horse chariots driven apart at speed had torn Mettus in two (you should have kept your word, man of Alba!), and Tullus was dragging the liar's entrails through the wood, and the spattered brambles dripped with blood.
sentences.n: Mettus (or Mettius) Fufetius, leader of Alba Longa, Rome's ally under its third king, Tullus Hostilius, held his army back in a battle to see which side would win, and Tullus had him tied between two four-horse chariots driven in opposite directions (Livy 1, from memory). 'citae… quadrigae', 'swift four-horse chariots', enclosing 'Mettum in diversa'. 'distulerant', 'had pulled apart', pluperfect: done before the moment shown. 'at tu dictis, Albane, maneres', 'but you, Alban, should have stood by your words', imperfect subjunctive of an obligation in the past not met; 'dictis' with 'maneo', 'abide by'. The poet turns aside to address the man, an apostrophe that draws the moral. 'viri mendacis', 'of the lying man'. 'raptabat', 'kept dragging', frequentative of 'rapio'. 'sparsi… vepres', 'the spattered brambles', framing. 'rorabant', 'were dripping like dew'. Elisions 'Mett(um) in', 'silv(am) et'.

sentences.t:
Nec non Tarquinium eiectum Porsenna iubebat
accipere ingentique urbem obsidione premebat:
sentences.l:
And also Tarquin, thrown out, Porsenna was ordering
to take back, and with a huge the city siege was pressing:
sentences.i: There too was Porsenna, ordering the Romans to take back the banished Tarquin and pressing the city with a great siege:
sentences.n: 'Nec non', 'and not not', i.e. 'and also'. Tarquinius Superbus, 'the Proud', seventh and last king of Rome, was driven out, by tradition in 509 BC, and the Republic began; Lars Porsenna, king of the Etruscan city of Clusium, took up his cause and besieged Rome (Livy 2, from memory). 'eiectum', 'thrown out', 'ej-ec-tum', with consonantal i after the prefix. 'iubebat accipere', 'was ordering (them) to receive', the Romans understood. 'ingenti… obsidione', 'with a huge siege', framing 'urbem'. The imperfects keep the picture in motion. Elisions 'Tarquini(um) eiectum', 'acciper(e) ingentique', 'ingentiqu(e) urbem', 'urb(em) obsidione'.

sentences.t: Aeneadae in ferrum pro libertate ruebant.
sentences.l: the sons of Aeneas onto the steel for freedom were rushing.
sentences.i: the sons of Aeneas were rushing onto the sword in the cause of freedom.
sentences.n: 'Aeneadae', 'sons of Aeneas', the Romans as his descendants, a patronymic; 'Ae-' is one syllable, the diphthong. 'in ferrum… ruebant', 'were rushing onto the steel', into battle. 'pro libertate', 'for freedom': freedom from kings, the watchword of the new Republic. Elision 'Aenead(ae) in'.

sentences.t:
Illum indignanti similem similemque minanti
aspiceres, pontem auderet quia vellere Cocles
et fluvium vinclis innaret Cloelia ruptis.
sentences.l:
Him like one in a rage and like one threatening
you would have seen, because the bridge dared to tear down Cocles
and the river, her bonds broken, swam Cloelia.
sentences.i: You could see Porsenna looking like a man in a fury, like a man uttering threats, because Cocles dared to tear down the bridge, and Cloelia had broken her bonds and was swimming the river.
sentences.n: 'Illum', Porsenna. 'indignanti similem similemque minanti', 'like one indignant and like one threatening', datives with 'similis', the two participles enclosing the repeated 'similem'. 'aspiceres', 'you would have seen', a past potential subjunctive addressed to any onlooker. Horatius Cocles ('the one-eyed') held the wooden bridge over the Tiber alone against the Etruscan army while the Romans cut it down behind him, then swam back across; Cloelia, a Roman girl given to Porsenna as a hostage, escaped and swam the Tiber, and Porsenna admired her courage (Livy 2, from memory). 'quia' is two short syllables, quĭ-ă. 'quia… auderet… innaret', 'because (he) dared… (she) swam', imperfect subjunctives: the cause is seen through Porsenna's resentment, or is drawn into the mood of 'aspiceres'. 'vinclis… ruptis', ablative absolute, 'her bonds broken'; 'vinclis', the short form of 'vinculis'. Elisions 'Ill(um) indignanti', 'pont(em) auderet'.

sentences.t:
In summo custos Tarpeiae Manlius arcis
stabat pro templo et Capitolia celsa tenebat,
Romuleoque recens horrebat regia culmo.
sentences.l:
At the top, guardian of the Tarpeian, Manlius, citadel,
was standing before the temple and the Capitol high was holding,
and with Romulus's, fresh, bristled the palace thatch.
sentences.i: At the top stood Manlius, guardian of the Tarpeian citadel, before the temple, holding the lofty Capitol, and the palace of Romulus bristled with its fresh thatch.
sentences.n: Marcus Manlius, afterwards called Capitolinus, held the Capitol when the Gauls took the rest of Rome, by tradition in 390 BC (Livy 5, from memory). 'In summo', 'at the top', of the shield, the top of its rim and the summit of the hill at once. 'custos Tarpeiae… arcis', 'guardian of the Tarpeian citadel', framing 'Manlius': the citadel on the Capitol, named after Tarpeia, who betrayed it to the Sabines; 'Tarpeiae' with consonantal i, 'Tar-pe-jae'. 'pro templo', 'in front of the temple', of Jupiter on the Capitol. 'Capitolia', poetic plural. 'Romuleo… culmo', 'with Romulean thatch', framing: the straw hut said to be Romulus's, kept on the Capitol as a relic and re-thatched, hence 'recens', 'fresh', and 'horrebat', 'bristled'. 'regia', 'palace', a king's house of straw. Elision 'templ(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Atque hic auratis volitans argenteus anser
porticibus Gallos in limine adesse canebat.
sentences.l:
And here, through gilded fluttering, silver, a goose,
colonnades, the Gauls on the threshold to be present was crying.
sentences.i: And here a silver goose, fluttering through gilded colonnades, cried out that the Gauls were at the threshold.
sentences.n: When the Gauls climbed the Capitol by night, the dogs did not bark, but the geese sacred to Juno cackled and woke Manlius, who threw the first Gaul down (Livy 5, from memory). 'auratis… porticibus', 'through the gilded colonnades', framing across the line-end: the porches of the temple. 'argenteus', 'of silver', the goose worked in silver on gold. 'volitans', 'flitting', frequentative of 'volo'. 'canebat', 'was singing', the cackle taken as a warning, almost a prophecy. 'Gallos… adesse', accusative and infinitive. Elisions 'Atqu(e) hic', 'limin(e) adesse'.

sentences.t:
Galli per dumos aderant arcemque tenebant,
defensi tenebris et dono noctis opacae:
sentences.l:
The Gauls through the thickets were at hand and the citadel were holding,
protected by the darkness and the gift of night shadowy:
sentences.i: The Gauls were coming up through the brushwood and all but held the citadel, shielded by the darkness and the gift of the dusky night:
sentences.n: 'Galli', the Gauls, the Celtic people of northern Italy and beyond the Alps. 'per dumos', 'through the thickets', up the cliff face. 'aderant', 'were there'. 'arcem… tenebant', 'were holding the citadel', the imperfect of an action begun and not completed: they were on the point of taking it. 'defensi', 'protected'. 'dono noctis opacae', 'by the gift of shadowy night'. The colon opens the picture of the Gauls themselves. No elisions.

sentences.t:
aurea caesaries ollis atque aurea vestis,
virgatis lucent sagulis, tum lactea colla
auro innectuntur, duo quisque Alpina coruscant
gaesa manu, scutis protecti corpora longis.
sentences.l:
golden the hair to them and golden the clothing;
with striped they shine little cloaks; then milk-white necks
with gold are entwined; two each Alpine brandish
javelins in hand, with shields protected as to their bodies long.
sentences.i: their hair was gold and gold their clothing; they gleamed in striped cloaks, and their milk-white necks were ringed with gold; each brandished two Alpine javelins in his hand, his body protected by a long shield.
sentences.n: The Gauls in gold and silver on the shield. 'caesaries', 'flowing hair': the Gauls were fair. 'ollis', the archaic form of 'illis', 'to them', dative of possession ('they had golden hair'). The verb 'erat' is left out. 'virgatis… sagulis', 'with striped little cloaks', 'sagulum' a diminutive of 'sagum', a soldier's cloak; the Gauls wore striped and checked cloth. 'lucent', 'they shine', the present breaking into the imperfects. 'lactea colla', 'milk-white necks', 'auro innectuntur', 'are bound with gold', the torques, twisted gold neck-rings. 'gaesa', a Gallic word, heavy iron javelins. 'Alpina', 'Alpine', from the mountains. 'duo quisque', 'each two'. 'corpora', accusative of respect with 'protecti', 'protected as to their bodies', a Greek construction. 'scutis… longis', framing. Elisions 'atqu(e) aurea', 'aur(o) innectuntur', 'quisqu(e) Alpina'.

sentences.t:
Hic exsultantis Salios nudosque Lupercos
lanigerosque apices et lapsa ancilia caelo
extuderat, castae ducebant sacra per urbem
pilentis matres in mollibus.
sentences.l:
Here the leaping Salii and the naked Luperci
and the wool-bearing caps and the fallen shields from the sky
he had hammered out; chaste were leading the sacred things through the city
in carriages the mothers, soft.
sentences.i: Here he had hammered out the leaping Salii and the naked Luperci, the wool-tufted caps, and the shields that fell from heaven; chaste matrons in cushioned carriages were leading the holy processions through the city.
sentences.n: The Salii, 'leapers', priests of Mars, danced through Rome each March carrying the 'ancilia', shields shaped like a figure of eight: one fell from the sky in the reign of King Numa as a pledge of Rome's safety, and eleven copies were made to hide the true one (Ovid, Fasti 3, from memory). The Luperci ran almost naked round the Palatine at the Lupercalia in February, striking people with goatskin thongs. 'lanigeros apices', 'wool-bearing caps', the 'apex', a priest's cap topped with a spike bound in wool. 'extuderat', 'had hammered out'. 'pilentis… in mollibus', 'in soft carriages', the 'pilentum', a cushioned carriage that Roman matrons were allowed to ride in at festivals, said to reward the gold they gave for the offering to Apollo vowed at Veii (Livy 5, from memory). Elisions 'lanigerosqu(e) apices', 'laps(a) ancilia'.

sentences.t:
Hinc procul addit
Tartareas etiam sedes, alta ostia Ditis,
et scelerum poenas et te, Catilina, minaci
pendentem scopulo Furiarumque ora trementem,
secretosque pios, his dantem iura Catonem.
sentences.l:
From here far off he adds
the Tartarean also seats, the deep doorways of Dis,
and of crimes the punishments, and you, Catiline, on a threatening
hanging crag and of the Furies the faces trembling at,
and the righteous set apart, to these giving laws Cato.
sentences.i: Far off from these he adds the abodes of Tartarus too, the deep gates of Dis, and the punishments of crime; and you, Catiline, hanging from a menacing crag and quaking at the faces of the Furies; and, set apart, the righteous, with Cato giving them laws.
sentences.n: The underworld, now on the shield. 'Hinc procul', 'far from here'. 'addit', a vivid present after the pluperfects. 'Tartareas… sedes', the place of punishment. 'Ditis', of Dis, god of the dead. Lucius Sergius Catilina, Catiline, a patrician who plotted to seize power at Rome in 63 BC and, exposed by Cicero, died in battle the next year: the type of the traitor. 'te, Catilina', apostrophe. 'minaci… scopulo', 'from a threatening crag', framing 'pendentem'. 'Furiarum… ora trementem', 'trembling at the Furies' faces', 'tremo' with the accusative. 'secretos… pios', 'the righteous apart', in Elysium. 'his dantem iura Catonem', 'Cato giving them laws': most take him as Cato the Younger, who killed himself in 46 BC rather than accept Julius Caesar's pardon, and who spoke hardest against Catiline's accomplices (Sallust, from memory); some think of Cato the Censor. Elisions 'alt(a) ostia', 'Furiarumqu(e) ora'.

sentences.t:
Haec inter tumidi late maris ibat imago
aurea, sed fluctu spumabant caerula cano;
sentences.l:
These among, of the swelling far-and-wide sea went the image,
golden, but with wave were foaming the blue waters, white;
sentences.i: Among these scenes ran the image of the wide and swelling sea, in gold, yet its blue waters foamed with white-crested waves;
sentences.n: 'Haec inter', 'among these', 'inter' after its object. 'tumidi late maris', 'of the sea swelling far and wide': 'lātē' is long in both syllables, 'măris' short in both. 'ibat', 'was going', ran round: the sea forms a band about the central scene. 'imago aurea', 'a golden image', worked in gold. 'sed', 'but': though the metal is gold, the eye sees blue water and white foam. 'caerula', neuter plural as a noun, 'the blue (waters)'. 'fluctu… cano', 'with white wave', framing. No elisions.

sentences.t:
et circum argento clari delphines in orbem
aequora verrebant caudis aestumque secabant.
sentences.l:
and round about, in silver bright, dolphins in a circle
the seas were sweeping with their tails and the surge were cutting.
sentences.i: and all round, dolphins bright in silver swept the waters in a circle with their tails and cut through the swell.
sentences.n: 'circum', adverb, 'round about'. 'argento clari', 'bright with silver', the dolphins worked in silver. 'delphines', a Greek form, three syllables. 'in orbem', 'in a circle', following the round of the shield. 'verrebant… secabant', 'were sweeping… were cutting', imperfects of continuing movement, as if the picture moved. 'aestum', 'the surge', the heaving of the sea. Elision 'circ(um) argento'.

sentences.t:
In medio classis aeratas, Actia bella,
cernere erat, totumque instructo Marte videres
fervere Leucaten auroque effulgere fluctus.
sentences.l:
In the middle the fleets bronze-beaked, the Actian war,
to see it was, and all, with Mars drawn up, you would see
to seethe Leucate, and with gold to blaze the waves.
sentences.i: In the centre could be seen the bronze-beaked fleets, the war of Actium: you could see all Leucate seething with the ranks of battle, and the waves ablaze with gold.
sentences.n: The centre of the shield: the battle of Actium, 2 September 31 BC, off the headland of Actium in north-western Greece, where Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra and made Octavian master of the Roman world. 'classis aeratas', 'the bronze-fitted fleets', '-is' accusative plural, ships with bronze rams. 'Actia bella', 'the Actian war', in apposition, plural for singular. 'cernere erat', 'it was (possible) to see', a Greek idiom. 'instructo Marte', ablative absolute, 'Mars drawn up', i.e. the battle in array, Mars standing for war. 'videres', 'you would have seen', past potential subjunctive. 'Leucaten', Greek accusative of 'Leucates', the headland of the island of Leucas south of Actium, for the whole stretch of sea; 'Leu-' is one syllable. 'fervere', 'to seethe'. Elisions 'cerner(e) erat', 'totumqu(e) instructo', 'auroqu(e) effulgere'.

sentences.i: On one side Augustus Caesar, leading the Italians into battle with the Senate and the people, the household gods and the great gods, stands high on the stern;
sentences.n: 'Hinc', 'on this side'. 'Augustus… Caesar', spanning the line: Octavian, great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar; he took the name Augustus, 'revered', in 27 BC, four years after Actium, and Virgil gives it to him here. 'Italos', Italy united against the East. 'cum patribus populoque', 'with the fathers and the people', the Senate and People of Rome. 'penatibus et magnis dis', 'with the Penates and the great gods', 'dis' = 'deis'; the same words end 3.12, 'cum sociis natoque Penatibus et magnis dis', where Aeneas sails from Troy with his household gods: Augustus fights with the gods Aeneas brought. The line closes with a spondee in the fifth foot and a single-syllable word, an old, weighty rhythm. 'stans celsa in puppi', 'standing on the high stern', the commander's post; there is no main verb. Elision 'cels(a) in'.

sentences.t:
geminas cui tempora flammas
laeta vomunt patriumque aperitur vertice sidus.
sentences.l:
twin, whose temples, flames
joyful spew out, and his father's is revealed on his head the star.
sentences.i: from his glad brows pour twin flames, and above his head his father's star shines out.
sentences.n: 'cui', 'for whom', dative of reference, here 'whose', with 'tempora', 'temples' of the head. 'geminas… flammas… vomunt', 'spew twin flames', a sign of divine favour, as when flame played round Ascanius's head at Troy (2.682–684). 'laeta', 'glad', with 'tempora'. 'patrium… sidus', 'his father's star', the comet that appeared during the games held after Julius Caesar's murder in 44 BC, taken as his soul received among the gods; Octavian, his adopted son, set it on his coins. 'vertice', 'on his head', ablative of place. 'aperitur', 'is disclosed', shines forth. Elision 'patriumqu(e) aperitur'.

sentences.t:
Parte alia ventis et dis Agrippa secundis
arduus agmen agens;
sentences.l:
In another part, with winds and gods favouring, Agrippa,
towering, the column leading;
sentences.i: Elsewhere Agrippa, with the winds and the gods to favour him, towers above the squadron he leads;
sentences.n: 'Parte alia', 'in another part'. Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Octavian's friend and admiral, who commanded the fleet at Actium. 'ventis et dis… secundis', ablative absolute, 'the winds and gods being favourable', framing 'Agrippa'. 'arduus', 'lofty', standing tall on his ship. 'agmen agens', 'leading the column', a sound-play on the same root. Again no main verb is expressed. Elision 'Part(e) alia'.

sentences.t:
cui, belli insigne superbum,
tempora navali fulgent rostrata corona.
sentences.l:
to whom, of war the decoration proud,
the temples with the naval shine, beaked, crown.
sentences.i: and on his brows gleams the naval crown, beaked like a ship, the proud distinction he won in war.
sentences.n: 'cui… tempora', 'whose temples', as at 680. 'belli insigne superbum', 'a proud badge of war', in apposition to the crown. 'navali… corona', 'with the naval crown', framing: a gold wreath set with ships' beaks, awarded to Agrippa for his victory over Sextus Pompeius at Naulochus in 36 BC (from memory). 'rostrata', 'beaked', agrees in grammar with 'tempora' but in sense belongs to the crown, a transferred epithet. Elision 'bell(i) insigne'.

sentences.t:
Hinc ope barbarica variisque Antonius armis,
victor ab Aurorae populis et litore rubro,
Aegyptum viresque Orientis et ultima secum
Bactra vehit, sequiturque (nefas) Aegyptia coniunx.
sentences.l:
On this side, with wealth barbaric and varied Antonius arms,
victor from the Dawn's peoples and the shore red,
Egypt and the strength of the East and the farthest with him
Bactra carries, and there follows (a sin!) an Egyptian wife.
sentences.i: On the other side is Antony, with barbaric wealth and a medley of arms, come in victory from the peoples of the Dawn and the shores of the Red Sea, bringing with him Egypt, the power of the East and Bactra at the world's end; and after him — an outrage! — follows his Egyptian wife.
sentences.n: Mark Antony, Octavian's partner and then rival, who ruled the eastern half of the Roman world from Alexandria with Cleopatra, queen of Egypt. 'Hinc', now the other side. 'ope barbarica variisque… armis', 'with barbarian wealth and varied arms', framing 'Antonius'. 'victor ab Aurorae populis', 'victor from the peoples of the Dawn', the East. 'litore rubro', 'from the red shore', of the Red Sea, which for the Romans took in the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean. 'ultima… Bactra', 'farthest Bactra', framing across the line-end, the capital of Bactria in Central Asia, at the edge of the known world. 'nefas', 'a sin!', an exclamation in brackets: a Roman with a foreign queen as his wife. 'Aegyptia coniunx', Cleopatra, never named in the poem; 'coniunx' with consonantal i. Elisions 'variisqu(e) Antonius', 'viresqu(e) Orientis'.

sentences.t:
Una omnes ruere, ac totum spumare reductis
convolsum remis rostrisque tridentibus aequor.
sentences.l:
Together all rush, and the whole foams, by drawn-back
torn up, oars and by beaks three-pronged, the sea.
sentences.i: All charge at once, and the whole sea foams, churned up by the sweep of the oars and the three-pronged rams.
sentences.n: 'ruere… spumare', historic infinitives: infinitives used as main verbs in lively narrative, with the subjects in the nominative ('omnes', 'aequor'), standing for imperfects. 'Una', 'together'. 'reductis… remis', 'by oars drawn back', the stroke. 'convolsum', Greenough's spelling of 'convulsum', 'torn up'. 'rostris… tridentibus', 'by three-toothed beaks', the bronze rams with three blades. 'totum… aequor', 'the whole sea', spanning the two lines. Elisions 'Un(a) omnes', 'ruer(e) ac'.

sentences.t: alta petunt:
sentences.l: The open sea they make for:
sentences.i: They make for the open sea:
sentences.n: The print has 'alta', lowercase after the full stop that ends 690, a misprint for 'Alta', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'alta petunt', 'they seek the deep', the open water, for room to fight. 'alta', neuter plural of 'altus' as a noun. No elisions.

sentences.t:
pelago credas innare revolsas
Cycladas aut montis concurrere montibus altos,
tanta mole viri turritis puppibus instant.
sentences.l:
on the sea you would think swam, torn loose,
the Cyclades, or mountains clashed with mountains high,
with such bulk the men on towered sterns press on.
sentences.i: you would think the Cyclades had been torn from their roots and were floating on the sea, or that high mountains were crashing into mountains, so huge are the towered ships from which the men press their attack.
sentences.n: 'credas', 'you would think', potential subjunctive with the generic 'you', taking two accusatives and infinitives. 'pelago… innare', 'to swim on the sea', 'pelago' dative with the compound verb (or ablative of place). 'revolsas Cycladas', 'the Cyclades torn loose', the ring of islands in the Aegean; 'revolsas', Greenough's spelling of 'revulsas'; 'Cycladas', Greek accusative plural. 'montis… altos', '-is' accusative plural, framing. 'tanta mole', 'with such great bulk', ablative of manner, explaining the comparison. 'turritis puppibus', 'with towered sterns', ships carrying wooden towers for archers; Antony's ships were famous for their size (Plutarch, from memory). 'instant', 'press on'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
stuppea flamma manu telisque volatile ferrum
spargitur, arva nova Neptunia caede rubescunt.
sentences.l:
Tow-fed flame by hand and with darts the flying steel
is scattered; the fields, with new, of Neptune, slaughter redden.
sentences.i: Blazing tow is flung by hand and flying steel in showers of missiles; the fields of Neptune redden with fresh slaughter.
sentences.n: The print has 'stuppea', lowercase after the full stop that ends 693, a misprint for 'Stuppea', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'stuppea flamma', 'flame of tow', burning hemp thrown to set the ships on fire. 'telis… volatile ferrum', 'flying iron with missiles', arrows and javelins. 'spargitur', 'is scattered', singular, agreeing with the nearer subject. 'arva… Neptunia', 'the fields of Neptune', the sea. 'nova… caede', 'with new slaughter'. 'rubescunt', 'grow red', an inceptive verb in '-sco'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Regina in mediis patrio vocat agmina sistro
necdum etiam geminos a tergo respicit anguis.
sentences.l:
The queen, in the midst, with her native calls the columns rattle,
and not yet even the twin behind her looks back at snakes.
sentences.i: In the thick of the fight the queen calls up her squadrons with the rattle of her native land, and does not yet look back to see the two snakes behind her.
sentences.n: 'Regina', Cleopatra, again unnamed. 'patrio… sistro', 'with her ancestral sistrum', framing: the bronze rattle shaken in the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis; Virgil gives her a temple instrument in place of a war-trumpet. 'necdum etiam', 'and not yet even'. 'geminos… anguis', 'the twin snakes', '-is' accusative plural: the death to come. After the defeat she killed herself at Alexandria in 30 BC, by the bite of a snake, as the story was told, and Octavian's triumph carried an image of her with the snake (Plutarch, from memory). 'a tergo', 'behind her'. 'respicit', 'looks back at'. Elisions 'Regin(a) in', 'necd(um) etiam'.

sentences.t:
omnigenumque deum monstra et latrator Anubis
contra Neptunum et Venerem contraque Minervam
tela tenent.
sentences.l:
And of every kind of gods monsters and the barker Anubis
against Neptune and Venus and against Minerva
weapons hold.
sentences.i: Monstrous gods of every shape, and Anubis the barker, take up arms against Neptune and Venus and against Minerva.
sentences.n: The print has 'omnigenumque', lowercase after the full stop that ends 697, a misprint for 'Omnigenumque', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'omnigenum… deum', 'of gods of every kind', both old genitive plurals in '-um' (= 'omnigenorum deorum'). 'monstra', 'monsters', the animal-headed gods of Egypt, strange to Roman eyes. 'latrator Anubis', 'the barker Anubis', the dog- or jackal-headed god who guided the dead. 'contra… contra', the gods of Egypt face the gods of Rome: Neptune, Venus, mother of the Julian line, and Minerva. 'tela tenent', 'hold weapons', fight. Elisions 'monstr(a) et', 'Neptun(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Saevit medio in certamine Mavors
caelatus ferro tristesque ex aethere Dirae,
et scissa gaudens vadit Discordia palla,
quam cum sanguineo sequitur Bellona flagello.
sentences.l:
Rages in the middle of the struggle Mavors,
engraved in iron, and the grim from the sky Dirae,
and, with torn rejoicing, strides Discord, cloak,
whom with bloody follows Bellona whip.
sentences.i: In the middle of the struggle Mars rages, engraved in iron, and with him the grim Furies from the sky above; Discord strides along exulting in her torn cloak, and Bellona follows her with a bloody whip.
sentences.n: 'Mavors', the old name of Mars, god of war. 'caelatus ferro', 'engraved in iron', a reminder that this is metalwork. 'Dirae', 'the Dread Ones', the Furies; 'ex aethere', 'from the upper air'. 'scissa… palla', 'with torn robe', framing, ablative with 'gaudens', 'rejoicing in'. 'Discordia', Strife as a goddess. 'quam', 'whom', relative, object of 'sequitur'. 'Bellona', the old Roman goddess of war; 'cum sanguineo… flagello', 'with a bloody scourge', framing. Elisions 'medi(o) in', 'tristesqu(e) ex'.

sentences.t:
Actius haec cernens arcum tendebat Apollo
desuper:
sentences.l:
Actian, seeing these things, his bow was bending, Apollo,
from above:
sentences.i: Seeing this, Apollo of Actium was bending his bow from on high:
sentences.n: 'Actius… Apollo', 'Actian Apollo', framing the line: Apollo had an old temple on the headland of Actium; Octavian claimed him as his patron, enlarged that temple after the victory, and built him a new one on the Palatine (the 'Phoebus' of 720). 'haec cernens', 'seeing these things'. 'arcum tendebat', 'was stretching his bow'. 'desuper', 'from above'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
omnis eo terrore Aegyptus et Indi,
omnis Arabs, omnes vertebant terga Sabaei.
sentences.l:
all, from that terror, Egypt and the Indians,
all the Arab, all were turning their backs, the Sabaeans.
sentences.i: at the terror of it, all Egypt and the Indians, every Arab, and all the Sabaeans turned and fled.
sentences.n: 'eo terrore', 'by that terror', ablative of cause. 'omnis… omnis… omnes', the repeated word sweeping up the whole East; 'omnis', nominative singular, with 'Aegyptus' (feminine) and with 'Arabs'. 'Indi', 'Indians', loosely, the peoples of the far East. 'Arabs', singular for the people. 'Sabaei', the people of Saba (Sheba) in southern Arabia, famous for incense. 'vertebant terga', 'were turning their backs', fleeing; the verb is plural for all the subjects. In 'Aegyptus' the 'Ae-' is one syllable. Elision 'terror(e) Aegyptus'.

sentences.t:
Ipsa videbatur ventis regina vocatis
vela dare et laxos iam iamque inmittere funis.
sentences.l:
Herself was seen, the winds called upon, the queen,
the sails to give and the slackened now, now to let go ropes.
sentences.i: The queen herself could be seen calling on the winds, setting sail, and at any moment letting the sheets run slack.
sentences.n: 'Ipsa… regina', 'the queen herself', framing: in the battle Cleopatra's squadron broke away and fled for Egypt, and Antony followed her (Plutarch, from memory). 'videbatur', 'was seen', with the infinitives 'dare… inmittere'. 'ventis… vocatis', ablative absolute, 'the winds having been called on'. 'vela dare', 'to give the sails' (to the wind), to set sail. 'iam iamque', 'now, at any moment'. 'laxos… funis', 'slackened ropes', '-is' accusative plural, framing; 'inmittere', Greenough's spelling of 'immittere', 'to let go'. Elisions 'dar(e) et', 'iamqu(e) inmittere'.

sentences.t:
Illam inter caedes pallentem morte futura
fecerat Ignipotens undis et Iapyge ferri,
sentences.l:
Her, amid the slaughter, pale with death to come,
had made the Fire-lord by the waves and by Iapyx to be borne,
sentences.i: The lord of fire had shown her amid the carnage, pale with the death to come, swept along by the waves and the west-north-west wind,
sentences.n: A comma-ended unit: the sentence runs to 713. 'Illam', Cleopatra. 'inter caedes', 'amid the slaughter', plural for the many killings. 'pallentem morte futura', 'pale with the death to come', ablative of cause. 'fecerat… ferri', 'had made her to be carried', the present passive infinitive. 'Ignipotens', Vulcan, here with a capital (lowercase at 628). 'Iapyge', 'by Iapyx', the west-north-west wind blowing from Iapygia (Apulia), which would carry a ship from Actium south-east towards Egypt; four syllables, Ĭ-ā-py̆-gĕ, the I a short vowel, so 'et' before it stays short. Elision 'Ill(am) inter'.

sentences.t:
contra autem magno maerentem corpore Nilum
pandentemque sinus et tota veste vocantem
caeruleum in gremium latebrosaque flumina victos.
sentences.l:
and opposite, the grieving with his great body Nile,
and spreading his folds and with all his robe calling
into his blue bosom and his hiding streams the conquered.
sentences.i: and facing her the Nile, his whole vast body grieving, opening the folds of his robe and with all its breadth calling the defeated into his dark-blue lap and the hiding-places of his waters.
sentences.n: 'contra autem', 'and opposite'. 'Nilum', the Nile as a river-god, the next object of 'fecerat', with three participles. 'magno maerentem corpore', 'grieving with his great body', framing: the whole huge figure mourns. 'pandentem… sinus', 'spreading the folds' of his robe, to shelter the fugitives. 'tota veste vocantem', 'calling with all his robe', beckoning with it. 'caeruleum in gremium', 'into his blue lap'. 'latebrosa… flumina', 'his streams full of hiding-places', the many channels of the Nile delta. 'victos', 'the conquered', object of 'vocantem'. Elisions 'contr(a) autem', 'caerule(um) in'.

sentences.t:
At Caesar, triplici invectus Romana triumpho
moenia, dis Italis votum inmortale sacrabat,
maxuma tercentum totam delubra per urbem.
sentences.l:
But Caesar, in triple carried in, the Roman, triumph,
walls, to the gods of Italy a vow undying was consecrating,
the greatest, three hundred, through the whole shrines city.
sentences.i: But Caesar, borne into the walls of Rome in a triple triumph, was dedicating an undying offering to the gods of Italy, three hundred great shrines throughout the city.
sentences.n: 'At', 'but': the scene moves to Rome. In August 29 BC Octavian held three triumphs on three days running, for Illyricum, for Actium and for Egypt. 'triplici… triumpho', framing; 'invectus… Romana… moenia', 'carried into the Roman walls', for the victorious general rode into the city in a chariot. 'dis Italis', 'to the gods of Italy', 'dis' = 'deis'. 'votum inmortale', 'an undying vow', the thing vowed, here temples that will last; 'inmortale', Greenough's spelling of 'immortale'. 'maxuma… delubra', 'the greatest shrines', in apposition to 'votum'; 'maxuma', Greenough's 'maxima'. 'tercentum', 'three hundred', a round number for very many; Augustus records that he restored eighty-two temples in a single year (Res Gestae, from memory). 'sacrabat', 'was consecrating', the imperfect of the scene in progress. Elisions 'triplic(i) invectus', 'vot(um) inmortale'.

sentences.t: Laetitia ludisque viae plausuque fremebant;
sentences.l: With gladness and games the streets and applause were roaring;
sentences.i: The streets rang with rejoicing, with games and applause;
sentences.n: 'Laetitia ludisque… plausuque', ablatives of cause with 'fremebant', 'were roaring', the double '-que'. 'viae', 'the streets'. 'ludis', the public games held to celebrate the victory. No elisions.

sentences.t: omnibus in templis matrum chorus, omnibus arae;
sentences.l: in all the temples of mothers a choir, in all altars;
sentences.i: in every temple there was a choir of matrons, in every temple altars;
sentences.n: The verbs ('erat', 'erant') are left out. 'omnibus… omnibus', the repeated word. 'matrum chorus', 'a choir of mothers', married women singing hymns of thanksgiving. 'arae', altars set up for sacrifice. No elisions.

sentences.t: ante aras terram caesi stravere iuvenci.
sentences.l: before the altars the ground, slain, strewed bullocks.
sentences.i: and before the altars the slaughtered bullocks covered the ground.
sentences.n: 'stravere' = 'straverunt', 'strewed', the '-ere' perfect (as always). 'terram… stravere', 'they strewed the ground', covered it with their bodies. 'caesi… iuvenci', 'slain young bulls', framing, the thank-offerings. 'iuvenci' with consonantal i. Elision 'ant(e) aras'.

sentences.i: He himself, seated on the snow-white threshold of shining Phoebus, reviews the gifts of the nations and fastens them to the proud doorposts;
sentences.n: 'Ipse', Caesar. 'niveo… limine', 'on the snowy threshold', framing: the temple of Apollo on the Palatine, built of gleaming white marble and dedicated in 28 BC, the year after the triumph; Virgil puts the two together. 'candentis… Phoebi', 'of shining Phoebus', Apollo. 'recognoscit', 'reviews', inspects, as a general checks the spoils. 'dona… populorum', 'the gifts of the peoples', the offerings of the conquered and of the cities. 'aptat… superbis postibus', 'fits to the proud doorposts', hanging up offerings on the temple. Elision 'populor(um) aptatque'.

sentences.t:
incedunt victae longo ordine gentes,
quam variae linguis, habitu tam vestis et armis.
sentences.l:
march in the conquered in a long line nations,
as varied in tongues, so in fashion of dress and in arms.
sentences.i: the conquered nations file past in a long procession, as varied in their dress and weapons as in their languages.
sentences.n: 'incedunt', 'step in procession', the captive peoples led in the triumph. 'victae… gentes', 'the conquered nations', framing. 'longo ordine', 'in a long line'. 'quam… tam', 'as… so', 'as varied in tongues as in style of dress and in arms'. 'linguis', 'habitu', 'armis', ablatives of respect; 'habitu… vestis', 'in the fashion of their clothing'. Elision 'long(o) ordine'.

sentences.i: Here Vulcan had modelled the Numidian race and the loose-robed Africans, here the Leleges and the Carians and the Geloni with their arrows;
sentences.n: 'Mulciber', an old name of Vulcan. 'finxerat', 'had moulded'. 'Nomadum genus', 'the race of the Nomads', the Numidians of North Africa; 'Nomadum' genitive plural. 'discinctos… Afros', 'the ungirt Africans', in loose robes worn without a belt, to a Roman eye a mark of softness; framing 'Mulciber'. 'Lelegas Carasque', Greek accusatives plural, two peoples of the south-west coast of Asia Minor. 'sagittiferos… Gelonos', 'the arrow-bearing Geloni', a Scythian people north of the Black Sea. The double '-que'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Euphrates ibat iam mollior undis,
extremique hominum Morini, Rhenusque bicornis,
indomitique Dahae, et pontem indignatus Araxes.
sentences.l:
the Euphrates was going now gentler in its waves,
and the farthest of men, the Morini, and the Rhine two-horned,
and the untamed Dahae, and, resenting its bridge, the Araxes.
sentences.i: the Euphrates now flowed with humbler waters; and there were the Morini, remotest of men, and the two-horned Rhine, and the untamed Dahae, and the Araxes, resentful of the bridge laid over it.
sentences.n: The rivers appear as figures, as images of conquered rivers were carried in Roman triumphs. 'Euphrates', the great river of Mesopotamia, the frontier with Parthia; 'Eu-' is one syllable, Eu-phrā-tēs. 'mollior undis', 'softer in its waves', humbled; 'undis', ablative of respect. 'extremi hominum Morini' (ex-trē-mī, hŏ-mĭ-num), 'the Morini, farthest of men', 'hominum' partitive genitive; they lived on the Channel coast of Gaul. 'Rhenus bicornis', 'the two-horned Rhine', a horned river-god, for its two mouths. 'Dahae', nomads east of the Caspian Sea. 'pontem indignatus Araxes', 'the Araxes resenting its bridge', a river of Armenia, said to have swept away a bridge built by Alexander (Servius, from memory). Not all of these had been conquered by 29 BC: the shield gathers the whole world into the triumph. Elisions 'extremiqu(e) hominum', 'Dah(ae) et', 'pont(em) indignatus'.

sentences.t:
Talia per clipeum Volcani, dona parentis,
miratur rerumque ignarus imagine gaudet,
attollens umero famamque et fata nepotum.
sentences.l:
Such things across the shield of Vulcan, the gift of his mother,
he marvels at, and of the events unknowing in the image rejoices,
lifting on his shoulder both the fame and the fates of his descendants.
sentences.i: Such are the scenes he marvels at across the shield of Vulcan, his mother's gift; he knows nothing of what they show, yet takes delight in the pictures, and he lifts onto his shoulder, with the shield, the renown and the destiny of the generations to come.
sentences.n: The last lines of Book 8. 'Talia', 'such things', object of 'miratur'. 'per clipeum', 'over the shield', his eyes travelling across it. 'Volcani', 'of Vulcan'. 'dona parentis', 'the gift of his parent', Venus, plural for singular, in apposition to 'clipeum'. 'rerum ignarus', 'not knowing the events', answering 'haud vatum ignarus' of Vulcan at 627: the maker knew; the bearer does not. 'imagine gaudet', 'rejoices in the picture', ablative of cause. 'attollens umero', 'lifting on his shoulder', the shield taken up to be carried. 'famamque et fata', 'both the fame and the fates', with the alliteration of f. 'nepotum', 'of descendants', literally 'grandsons'. At Troy Aeneas carried his father Anchises out of the burning city on his shoulders (2.707–708, 721–723); now he shoulders the future. Elisions 'rerumqu(e) ignarus', 'famamqu(e) et'.
